extraction.name: SWE-rebench
extraction.description: A public dataset comprising over 21,000 interactive Python-based software engineering tasks collected automatically from real-world GitHub repositories, suitable for reinforcement learning-based training and benchmarking of software engineering agents.
extraction.creator: Ibragim Badertdinov, Alexander Golubev, Maksim Nekrashevich, Anton Shevtsov, Simon Karasik, Andrei Andriushchenko, Maria Trofimova, Daria Litvintseva, Boris Yangel
extraction.citeAs: Badertdinov, Ibragim, Alexander Golubev, Maksim Nekrashevich, Anton Shevtsov, Simon Karasik, Andrei Andriushchenko, Maria Trofimova, Daria Litvintseva, and Boris Yangel. "SWE-rebench: An Automated Pipeline for Task Collection and Decontaminated Evaluation of Software Engineering Agents." arXiv:2505.20411v2, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was built with a fully automated four-stage pipeline: preliminary task collection, automated installation instruction configuration, execution-based installation verification, and automated instance quality assessment. Raw data were downloaded from GitHub Archive and GitHub, issues were linked with pull requests that mention resolving them, and filtering was applied to retain resolved Python repository issues with merged PRs, sufficient issue descriptions, test changes, and limited file changes. Remaining issues were treated as task instances, grouped by project version, and candidate environment setup instructions were generated with an LLM and iteratively refined using error logs. Tasks were then verified by executing tests in containers before and after applying solution patches, and quality labels were added using a fine-tuned model.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Web API, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The primary sources are GitHub Archive daily JSON archives of public GitHub events and GitHub repositories cloned with full commit histories. From GitHub Archive, the authors collected issue descriptions, discussions, linked pull requests, creation dates, labels, merge status, last commit, and discussions. From GitHub, they cloned relevant repositories to local storage for repository data access, pull request change identification, and version analysis.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Issues created before May 1, 2025 were used for the main dataset collection; benchmark tasks were filtered to issues created in 2025, with analyses on January 2025 and March-April 2025 subsets.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For each selected pull request, the overall patch was divided into a solution patch containing changes to non-test files and a test patch containing only changes to test files. Task instances were grouped by project versions inferred from git tags normalized to major.minor format; for each version group, the base_commit of the task instance with the most recent base_commit date was selected. If git tag did not provide a version, a unique version was assigned so the task used its own environment. Patch generation prioritized diffing head_commit against base_commit, with fallback to merge_commit if head_commit was unavailable. Deleted files were filtered out from test directives.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The pipeline merged raw inputs from multiple origins and applied preliminary filtering. Initial collection downloaded approximately 450,000 pull requests linked to issues from over 30,000 repositories with permissive licenses and more than 75% Python code. Filters required that the issue be from a Python repository with a permissive license, marked as resolved, linked to a PR merged into the main branch, not linked to multiple issues, have a description longer than 10 characters, include PRs that introduce or modify tests and include code changes beyond test files, and affect 1 to 15 files. During validation, environments were installed in isolated containers, tests were executed and parsed, exact dependency versions were recorded after successful setup, flaky tests were run multiple times and excluded if they failed in at least one run, and instances with validation failures were rejected.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset includes automated annotations for Issue Clarity, Task Complexity, and Test Patch Correctness. To produce these labels, the authors fine-tuned Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct using human annotations from SWE-bench Verified. For each of over 3,800 examples, the model received the issue description, canonical solution patch, and test patch, and was prompted to predict one of three binary quality labels. Each label was trained independently, and the resulting LLM-generated labels were provided as metadata with each task instance.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The quality assessment model was trained and evaluated with a 75/25 training/validation split, totaling 413 validation examples. Reported validation performance was 81% accuracy and weighted F1 0.82 for Task Complexity, 67% accuracy and weighted F1 0.65 for Test Patch Correctness, and 79% accuracy and weighted F1 0.76 for Issue Clarity. The paper notes that this automated assessment is not perfect and contains errors, but provides users with metadata for filtering tasks by quality characteristics.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Human annotations used for training came from SWE-bench Verified.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is described as a public dataset on Hugging Face Datasets, and the associated SWE-rebench leaderboard is continuously updated with fresh tasks collected using the same methodology. Future work includes keeping the benchmark up-to-date by maintaining evaluation on fresh tasks for existing models, evaluating a wider range of LLMs, and sharing detailed performance analyses with the community.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that SWE-rebench aims to accelerate open-source research and improve the reliability and performance of LLM-based software engineering agents. It also notes potential risks from accelerating increasingly autonomous AI systems in software engineering, such as overreliance on AI-generated code or misuse of automated agents for introducing vulnerabilities. The authors argue that openness, decontaminated evaluations, and rigorous benchmarking practices help mitigate these concerns and contribute to responsible advancement of the field.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is limited to Python repositories with permissive licenses and initially targets issue-linked pull requests from GitHub repositories where Python constitutes over 75% of the codebase. The automated pipeline relies on heuristics and LLM-driven interpretations, and the benchmark may contain imperfectly described or unsolvable tasks due to automated quality assessment errors. The paper also discusses contamination bias in older benchmarks and uses issue and pull request creation dates relative to model release dates to mark potentially contaminated evaluations.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The authors state that extracting consistently high-quality, verifiable tasks from diverse real-world GitHub repositories is inherently imperfect. The LLM-based installation instruction generation was validated on a limited set of 18 repositories for prompt engineering and may not capture every project's subtleties. Automated task quality assessment cannot fully replicate nuanced human judgment and contains errors, decreasing dataset quality. The fully automated pipeline may result in some tasks being imperfectly described or unsolvable solely from the issue, leading to lower absolute success rates compared to manually curated benchmarks. The initial release is limited exclusively to Python, restricting applicability to other language ecosystems.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed to train and benchmark software engineering agents in diverse executable environments and is particularly suitable for reinforcement learning-based approaches. The broader dataset contains 21,336 annotated task instances for training and evaluation, while a filtered benchmark subset of 294 executable tasks from 169 repositories is used for standardized model evaluation on the SWE-rebench leaderboard. The paper also notes that the quality labels can be used to filter tasks according to user criteria for model training or evaluation.
